主要内容: Foreign carmakers are increasingly targeting the U.S. sedan market as Detroit automakers shift focus toward SUVs and crossovers. Over the past decade, sedans, coupes, and other passenger cars accounted for more than half of the new vehicle market, but by the end of November 2018, that share had dropped to 30.5 percent. This decline is expected to continue for several more years. As the Detroit Big Three scale back sedan production, foreign competitors like Honda, Nissan, Toyota, and Audi are capitalizing on the opportunity. General Motors announced it would discontinue six popular sedans, while Ford had already planned to phase out most passenger cars, except for the Mustang. Fiat Chrysler has also moved in the same direction. However, some analysts question whether the Big Three are overreacting, as foreign automakers are also expanding their utility vehicle lines. For example, Hyundai, which saw a sharp decline in sales, has added three new utility vehicles, including the Palisade, the largest SUV it has ever offered. Meanwhile, Mercedes-Benz USA remains bullish on sedans, despite the industry trend. The Los Angeles Auto Show highlighted the shift, with many new SUVs and crossovers debuting, but also some new passenger cars like the updated Nissan Maxima and the redesigned Mazda3. Honda has maintained its presence in the sedan segment with models like the Accord and Civic, which are expected to sell at least 700,000 units in the U.S. this year. The company also introduced the new Insight hybrid, which was recognized as a finalist for the North American Car of the Year and the Green Car of the Year. Similarly, Toyota is reevaluating its sedan lineup, with CEO Jim Lentz acknowledging the need to focus on profitable segments. While overall light truck demand has kept auto sales from declining significantly, compact and midsize sedans have seen sharp declines, with Honda and Toyota experiencing drops of 12.6% and 17.3%, respectively. Despite these challenges, foreign automakers like Honda and Toyota continue to emphasize their commitment to sedans, highlighting the ongoing competition in the U.S. market.
